Easy sampled negatives can conceal catalog-ranking failures. Krichene and Rendle show sampled top-k metrics can reverse model comparisons even in expectation; smaller candidate sets also blur distinctions between metrics. [RecSys 2025 research](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748086) examines sampling reliability through model separability, agreement with full evaluation, robustness to exposure bias, and recovery of ground-truth rankings. A [sequential-recommendation study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.13045) finds both uniform and popularity-based candidate sampling can disagree with full-catalog model rankings. Popularity sampling therefore provides a useful stress test, not a guaranteed correction.

Practical diagnostic proposal: audit a fixed, bounded sample of training prefixes, scoring every eligible catalog item in chunks with the same trained HSTU model. Exclude padding and prefix-seen items while retaining the observed next-item target. Compute ranks by accumulating counts of scores greater than and equal to the target score; report optimistic/pessimistic tie bounds and tied-item counts without sorting the catalog. Stratify results by target popularity from training interactions and by negative difficulty, including title/description similarity. These strata are diagnostic suggestions, not findings established by the cited papers; unobserved items are not confirmed dislikes.

Repeat unique-candidate sampling on identical prefixes, reporting mean, dispersion, and top-10 hit-flip frequency across draws; separate candidate randomness from user-sampling uncertainty. Compare uniform, popularity-stratified, and text-similar candidate sets against exact ranks on that audit subset. [2024 rank-estimation research](https://research.google/pubs/improved-estimation-of-ranks-for-learning-item-recommenders-with-negative-sampling/) supports concern about negative-sampling bias, but repeated sampling alone does not remove it. Label all training-prefix results as in-sample diagnostics; preserve the host’s fixed validation HR@10 and macro-average as the selection criterion.
